title: The history of popcorn
tagline: Nearly 9,000 years from a wild grass to a snack that explodes in a pan, and 400 years of people wondering why.
intro: People in the Americas were popping corn thousands of years before anyone wrote about it. Machines, cinemas and microwaves made it a habit, and high-speed film in 2015 finally showed what happens in the few hundredths of a second when a kernel goes off.

eras.name: Corn that bursts
eras.summary: Maize is domesticated in Mexico, and people in Peru are popping it by about 4700 BCE.

eras.name: Written down
eras.summary: Aztec ceremonies and Spanish writers record the popped corn they saw in Mexico and Peru.

eras.name: Steam, crowds and cinemas
eras.summary: A Chicago inventor puts a popper on wheels, and popcorn follows the crowds to fairs and picture houses.

eras.name: Screens and bags
eras.summary: Television, brands and the microwave move popcorn into the home.

eras.name: Digging up the past
eras.summary: Archaeologists find old cobs in caves and coastal mounds.

eras.name: Science and snacks
eras.summary: Food chemists and physicists study the hull, the pressure and the jump, while the snack stays popular.

events.title: Early farmers domesticate maize
events.text: Wild grass called teosinte is bred into maize in the Balsas River valley of central Mexico. The Popcorn Board says it is believed that popping was the first thing people did with early corn.
events.why: Every popcorn kernel descends from this plant.

events.title: Oldest popcorn eaten in Peru
events.where: Paredones and Huaca Prieta, northern coast of Peru
events.text: Cobs, husks and stalks from these two coastal sites show people ate corn as popcorn and as flour. Radiocarbon dates reach back about 6,700 years. Corn was not yet a big part of the diet, and the find predates pottery in the region.
events.why: It is the oldest popcorn on record, found far from where maize began.

events.title: Popcorn in Aztec ceremonies
events.text: Popcorn was part of Aztec ceremonies. It decorated headdresses, necklaces and statues of gods, including Tlaloc, god of rain and fertility. Young women danced in garlands of popcorn.
events.why: Popcorn was a sacred food, not just a snack.

events.title: Cortés sees popcorn
events.text: The Popcorn Board says Cortés first saw popcorn when he invaded Mexico and met the Aztecs in 1519.
events.why: It is how many European writers first heard of it.

events.title: The Florentine Codex records Aztec life
events.who: Bernardino de Sahagún and Nahua authors and artists
events.text: A Spanish friar and a team of Nahua scholars and painters finish a 12-book illustrated encyclopedia of Aztec life, in Nahuatl and Spanish. The Popcorn Board quotes Sahagún's account of a popcorn dance.
events.why: Our best written picture of popcorn in Aztec life comes from this work and its Nahua authors.

events.title: Cobo writes of Peruvian popped corn
events.text: The Spanish writer Cobo describes Peruvians toasting a kind of corn until it bursts. They called it pisancalla and ate it as a sweet.
events.why: Popping was still a living tradition in the Andes.

events.title: The plough spreads maize farming
events.text: The steel moldboard plough comes into common use and maize planting spreads across the United States.
events.why: It prepared the farmland for a popcorn industry.

events.title: Cretors sets up a steam-powered roaster
events.text: Charles Cretors gets a peddler's licence and sets a steam-powered peanut roaster on the pavement outside his shop. This is the start of C. Cretors and Company.
events.why: The steam-powered machine he built is the ancestor of the popcorn machine.

events.title: Popcorn for breakfast
events.who: Ella Eaton Kellogg and John Harvey Kellogg
events.text: In the late 1800s and early 1900s, popcorn was eaten like cereal, ground up with milk or cream. Ella Kellogg liked it that way, and John Harvey Kellogg praised it as a whole grain.
events.why: Popcorn was once breakfast, long before the corn flake.

events.title: The first modern popcorn machine
events.text: Cretors adds a built-in popper to his peanut roaster and shows it at the World's Fair in Chicago. His company calls it the first modern popcorn machine. The Popcorn Board calls it the first mobile one. Street vendors soon wheel steam and gas poppers through fairs and parks.
events.why: Popcorn moved out of kitchens and on to the street.

events.title: First machine exported
events.text: The company sells its first export, a popcorn wagon, to the Netherlands for $400.
events.why: The idea spread beyond America.

events.title: A wagon with its own engine
events.text: Cretors introduces the first self-propelled popcorn wagon, driven by a petrol engine. The company calls it the first mobile concession stand.
events.why: The popcorn stand now travelled by itself.

events.title: Popcorn goes to the movies
events.text: Talking pictures make cinemas a fixture. At first many owners refuse to sell popcorn because it is messy, so vendors sell it outside. Cinemas that held out lost business, and popcorn machines moved into the lobby.
events.why: The cinema became popcorn's best home.

events.title: Popcorn thrives in the Great Depression
events.text: At 5 or 10 cents a bag, popcorn is one of the few treats poor families can afford. Sales rise while many other businesses fail.
events.why: Cheap and cheerful, popcorn became a habit.

events.title: Sugar shortage, popcorn boom
events.text: In the Second World War, sugar is sent overseas to troops, so there is less candy. Americans eat about three times as much popcorn as usual.
events.why: Wartime shortages made it a national snack.

events.title: Spencer files a patent for microwave cooking
events.text: Percy Spencer of Raytheon, who helped mass-produce magnetrons for radar, files a patent for cooking food with microwave energy. Popcorn is said to have been among his first test foods, though that part of the story is told as legend.
events.why: It led to the microwave oven, and later to microwave popcorn.

events.title: The first commercial microwave ovens
events.text: The first commercial microwave ovens stand about six feet tall, weigh around 750 pounds and cost about $5,000.
events.why: Microwave cooking began as an industrial machine.

events.title: Popcorn ears found in Bat Cave
events.who: Herbert W. Dick and Claude Earle Smith Jr.
events.where: Bat Cave, Catron County, New Mexico
events.text: Digs in a cave in west-central New Mexico turned up small ears of popcorn, from smaller than a penny to about two inches long. The Popcorn Board gives their age as about 4,000 years. Other sources give earlier or different dates, so the age is not settled.
events.why: It was long cited as the oldest popcorn, until the Peru finds.

events.title: Television cuts into popcorn
events.text: As television spreads, cinema visits fall, and popcorn sales fall with them. People then start to eat it at home in front of the TV, and sales recover.
events.why: The snack followed the screen from the cinema into the living room.

events.title: The RedBow hybrid
events.who: Orville Redenbacher, Charles Bowman and Carl Hartman
events.text: After years of cross-pollinating, three popcorn enthusiasts develop a hybrid that gives lighter, fluffier popcorn with few unpopped kernels. They sell it as RedBow.
events.why: Breeding, not just cooking, could cut the old maids.

events.title: A counter-top microwave for $495
events.text: A smaller counter-top Radarange goes on sale for about $495.
events.why: Ovens finally became cheap enough for kitchens.

events.title: Orville Redenbacher's Gourmet Popping Corn
events.text: The partners rename RedBow after Redenbacher and start selling gourmet popping corn. Both men were Purdue graduates who had gone into the seed business together.
events.why: A breeder's hybrid became a household brand.

events.title: The brand goes national
events.text: Redenbacher and Bowman turn their popcorn over to the food company Hunt-Wesson. Redenbacher becomes its spokesperson.
events.why: Advertising made popcorn a brand.

events.title: Microwave popcorn arrives
events.text: Microwave popcorn bags appear in the early 1980s, and home popcorn eating rises over the following years. Most microwave ovens now have a popcorn button.
events.why: Popcorn became a one-minute snack.

events.title: McClintock wins the Nobel Prize for work on maize
events.text: Barbara McClintock studied maize chromosomes and kernel colours. In the 1940s and 1950s she proved that genetic elements can change position on a chromosome. She won the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
events.why: Our deepest knowledge of the maize genome began with her.

events.title: Why the hull decides whether a kernel pops
events.who: Bruce Hamaker and colleagues, Purdue University
events.text: Purdue researchers compare 14 yellow popcorn varieties and find that from 4 to 47 percent of kernels stay unpopped. They say the hull's cellulose structure decides how well it holds moisture in, like a pressure cooker.
events.why: It pointed to a leaky hull as the cause of old maids.

events.title: Peru popcorn study published
events.who: Alex Grobman, Duccio Bonavia, Tom Dillehay, Dolores Piperno and colleagues
events.text: A team reports in the journal PNAS on corn remains from Paredones and Huaca Prieta that reach back about 6,700 years, and shows that people ate popcorn there.
events.why: It pushed the story of popcorn back by about two thousand years.

events.title: Virot and Ponomarenko explain the pop
events.text: Two physicists film kernels at about 2,900 frames per second. They find a critical temperature near 180 °C and a pressure near 10 bar, and show that the jump is driven by a leg of starch pushing on the surface. They suggest the pop sound comes from vapour release, and say this is consistent with their data but not proven.
events.why: It put numbers and film on a mystery as old as popcorn.

events.title: A popcorn ball that weighed 9,370 pounds
events.text: Volunteers at the Noble Popcorn plant build a popcorn ball almost 12 feet across, to win back the title of world's largest. It weighs 9,370 pounds, with almost five tons of popcorn in it.
events.why: A sign that the snack is still loved in the corn belt.

people.name: Charles Cretors
people.role: Inventor and founder of C. Cretors and Company
people.note: An Ohio-born craftsman who moved to Chicago in the 1880s and built the first modern popcorn machine.

people.name: Percy Spencer
people.note: Helped mass-produce radar magnetrons and filed the 1945 patent for microwave cooking.

people.name: Orville Redenbacher
people.note: Bred a hybrid popcorn and put his own name on it.

people.name: Barbara McClintock
people.note: Showed that genes can move on a chromosome, work that won her the 1983 Nobel Prize.

people.name: Ella Eaton Kellogg
people.note: Ate popcorn ground with milk as a breakfast food and urged others to eat it at meals.

people.name: Dolores Piperno
people.note: Co-author of the study of the Peruvian popcorn, and a leading voice on when and where maize was domesticated.

people.name: Antonio Valeriano
people.note: One of the Nahua authors named by the Getty as helping to create the Florentine Codex.

people.name: Bernardino de Sahagún
people.note: Led the team that compiled the Florentine Codex over thirty years.

people.name: Emmanuel Virot
people.note: Co-author of the 2015 study of why popcorn jumps and pops.

people.note: Co-author of the 2015 study of why popcorn jumps and pops.

series.title: Age of the oldest evidence found
series.caption: Each newly reported find pushed the story back. The 9,000-year point is for maize itself, not popcorn.

points.label: Bat Cave, New Mexico: popcorn ears about 4,000 years old
Maize domesticated in Mexico, nearly 9,000 years ago (not popcorn)

series.title: Price of a microwave oven
series.caption: Counter-top ovens became about ten times cheaper in twenty years.

facts: Popcorn is the only one of the main kinds of corn that pops. Its scientific name is Zea mays everta.
Kernels from burial grounds in northern Chile, about 1,000 years old, were still able to pop.
Popcorn needs about 13.5 to 14 percent moisture to pop well.
Popcorn is a whole grain, and Americans eat about 14 billion quarts of it a year (average of 2016 to 2020 sales).
